card.hook: From across the valley, Kiyomizu-dera's big wooden stage looks like it's floating out over the treetops. It's the shot everyone wants, and it's easier to get than you'd think.
card.stand_here: Head to Okuno-in (奥の院), across the ravine to the north of the Main Hall. Stand about 100 m east of the numbered pin and face west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole stage, the trees and the view behind. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the timber scaffolding. Save 0.5x for the pagoda or waterfall, when you want lots of foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stage, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker if the sky behind looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds build up around 10 a.m. Some guides also suggest the last hour before closing, so check the temple's official site for current opening times.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little higher than your face. Turn so the wooden stage sits over your shoulder, and keep your arm steady so you both stay in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the Main Hall's inner sanctum. Okuno-in is inside the paid temple grounds, so check the official site for admission, opening times and any renovation works.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the stage on the lower line, and see if you can get a shot with no stray heads or branches poking in.
card.good_to_know: Kiyomizu-dera means 'Pure Water Monastery', and it's part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto UNESCO World Heritage Site. The current Main Hall dates from 1633, after a fire in 1629. In the Edo period, people believed that surviving a 13-metre jump from the stage would grant a wish. 234 jumps were recorded, most were survived, and the practice was banned in 1872.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Okuno-in (奥の院), across the ravine to the north of the Main Hall. Stand about 100 m east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.

card.hook: Picture a pavilion with gold-leaf top floors, standing next to a second pavilion made entirely of water. That's Kinkaku-ji on a good day, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Head for Kinkaku-ji and stand about 100 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll be looking across the pond at the pavilion.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view across the water. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the gold floors. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of pond and trees, and keep the pavilion away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pavilion, then slide the brightness down a little so the gold keeps its detail instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Try the morning if you can. The gold often looks warm then, and the paths can be quieter. Bright days usually give a clearer reflection in the pond.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge that crosses Kyoko-chi (Mirror Pond) on the walking route. A guide describes it as a spot that frames the pavilion against the greenery. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the pavilion over your shoulder, and check the screen to make sure it's actually in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at the Mirror Pond viewing area directly across from the pavilion, on the opposite shore about 30 m from the water's edge near the main entrance, to shoot you with the pavilion and its reflection behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed only from the designated outside paths, and the interior is off limits. Selfie sticks and drones are prohibited. The garden is a one-way circuit, so you can't go back once you've passed a viewpoint. In crowds, step to the side instead of stopping in the middle of the path, and shoot quickly.
card.challenge: Get the gold pavilion and its shimmering twin in one frame, with a bit of pine branch in the foreground, and no strangers' elbows in the corners.
card.good_to_know: Kinkaku-ji's official name is Rokuon-ji, and it's a Zen Buddhist temple. The site began as a villa bought by the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu in 1397, and it became a temple after his death. The pavilion you see today is from 1955, rebuilt after a fire in 1950. It has three storeys and is about 12.5 metres tall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Kinkaku-ji and stand about 100 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll be looking across the pond at the pavilion.

card.hook: Imagine walking into a tunnel of bright vermilion gates that closes in around you, post after post, until the path seems to vanish. That's Fushimi Inari, and your camera roll is about to turn very orange-red.
card.stand_here: At Fushimi Inari Taisha, stand about 45 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the tower gate and shrine buildings. Switch to 0.5x in the gate tunnel to catch the full height of the posts and the length of the path. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for fox statues and lanterns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a mid-tone part of the gate, then slide to a little darker so the red stays rich and the shady tunnel doesn't look flat.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in your shots. Evening is lovely too, since the approach and main hall are lit through the night. Midday is the busiest and brightest.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Senbon Torii just behind the main hall, where the gates split into two parallel rows, and stand with the tunnel behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low so the packed gates fill the background. One guide suggests the right-hand path going up for a tighter frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so be respectful and don't block worshippers on the narrow paths. Skip the selfie stick on the Senbon Torii path, because the gates are tightly spaced and it gets crowded. Bring a flashlight for anything above the mid-mountain.
card.challenge: Find a fox statue, zoom to 2x, and see if you can get its stony stare in the same shot as a glowing red gate.
card.good_to_know: Fushimi Inari Taisha is the head shrine of Inari, the kami of rice and agriculture. The shrine is said to have around 10,000 gates, each donated by a Japanese business, and about 800 of them line the main path as the Senbon Torii. The main hall dates from 1499, and the foxes you'll spot everywhere are thought of as Inari's messengers.

card.hook: Picture about 130 shops squeezed into a lane so narrow that your elbows start apologising. That's Nishiki Market, Kyoto's kitchen, and it's a colourful mess in the best way.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, in the lane of Nishiki Market on Nishikikōji Street. Face along the lane, and keep to the side so shoppers can get past.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the view down the lane. If the arcade feels too tight, try 0.5x. Use 2x or more (depending on your phone) for food and signs, so you don't have to lean over the stalls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the middle of the lane on a vertical line, so the roof and shopfronts lead the eye away from you.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, so the lane is easier to photograph. The roof gives fairly even light at any hour, so you don't need sunshine.
card.selfie_here: Head to the market entrance and pose next to the Miffy statue holding a basket, which one guide calls a must-do photo stop. Or stand in the entrance itself, where the traditional wooden architecture makes a good backdrop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the entrance sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are highly discouraged here because the arcade is narrow. Don't block traffic while you shoot. Ask permission, or at least give a polite nod, before taking close-ups of vendors, stall owners or their goods.
card.challenge: Get three shots: one of the whole lane, one of a hand-written sign, and one of a tidy tray of pickles that makes you hungry.
card.good_to_know: Fish was being sold in this area as early as the year 782, helped by cold groundwater that kept it fresh. The market got official permission to sell fish in 1615. The cobbles under your feet were laid in 1984 and the roof followed in 1993, while the knife shop Aritsugu dates back to 1560.

card.hook: The floors inside Nijo Castle chirp when you walk on them, and that's not even the most dramatic thing here. Two rings of walls and wide moats mean you'll be snapping stone, water and timber before you know it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 240 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. That puts Nijo Castle's walls and moat right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the walls, moat and gate into one shot. Switch to 1x for most views, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for roof details and carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines so the walls and rooflines stay nice and level.
card.best_time: Early in the day usually means softer light and fewer people in your frame. Check the official site for current visiting times.
card.selfie_here: Head for the open plaza in front of Karamon Gate and turn your back on the carved gate. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the gate fits over your shoulder. For a different look, try the moat bank facing Higashi-Otemon Gate, where white walls and black tiles sit behind the water.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the open area between Karamon Gate and the Ninomaru Palace entrance, where the official site says group photos are fine as long as you don't block other visitors.
card.rules_and_safety: The castle asks visitors to avoid monopods on the grounds. In the Painting Gallery, flash and extended selfie sticks are prohibited too. Palace interiors may have their own photo rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Line up a stone wall with your gridlines, tuck a bit of moat water in the foreground, and see if you can get it perfectly straight in one go.
card.good_to_know: Ieyasu ordered Nijo Castle built in 1601 as the Kyoto home of the Tokugawa shoguns, and it was finished in 1626 under his grandson Iemitsu. It's one of the seventeen Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto on UNESCO's World Heritage list. The Ninomaru Palace is made almost entirely of Hinoki cypress, and its famous chirping floors are just clamps moving against nails, not an alarm.

card.hook: Picture a dance stage wrapped in rows of paper lanterns, all glowing against a sky that's just starting to go dark. Each lantern carries the name of someone who sponsors the festivals, so it's pretty up close too.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Maidono, the dance stage in the grounds beside the main hall at Yasaka Shrine. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the stage and keep it level in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole stage and all its lanterns in. Switch to 1x for a more natural view, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the names on the lanterns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the stage level, then tap a lantern and slide it a touch darker so the lights don't turn into white blobs.
card.best_time: Arrive as the light fades, so the lanterns are lit and the sky still has some colour. If you'd rather have fewer people in the shot, early morning is calmest, but the lanterns won't be glowing then.
card.selfie_here: Head to the stone steps in front of the West Gate (Nishiromon) on the Shijō-dōri side, which guides call the shrine's trademark photo spot. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and stand on the steps with the vermilion gate over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand at the foot of the stone steps and shoot upward while you stand on the steps, so the whole gate fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working Shinto shrine, so keep to the paths and be considerate of people who have come to pray. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a lantern with a name on it, then zoom in until you can fill the whole frame with just that one.
card.good_to_know: Yasaka Shrine is also known as Gion-san, and building began in 656. It's dedicated to Susanoo and tied to the Gion Matsuri every July. In April, crowds pass through on their way to Maruyama Park for the cherry blossom.

card.hook: Plot twist: the Silver Pavilion was never silver. It's a plain wooden building, and that quiet, unfinished look is exactly why it photographs so well.
card.stand_here: Stand about 55 m east of the Silver Pavilion and face west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the pavilion and the pond. Drop to 0.5x for the mossy garden and the sand garden, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for roof lines and sand textures.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pavilion, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and the pond reflection keep their detail.
card.best_time: Soft, even light suits the moss and the pavilion, so go early in the day or on a lightly overcast one. Damp weather can make the moss look richer, but keep your phone protected.
card.selfie_here: Head to the south end of Kinkyo-chi (Brocade Mirror Pond), where the pavilion sits among the greenery and the pond reflects it during the day. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and aim to get the pavilion over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in front of the Main Hall (Hojo) facing the Kannon-den, while you stand on the sand-garden side with the pavilion beyond you.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch your step on the moss-lined hillside stones, because they can be slippery when wet.
card.challenge: Take three shots in a row: one wide scene-setter, one of the moss, and one of the sand mound, then see which one you'd actually frame.
card.good_to_know: Ginkaku-ji's official name is Jishō-ji, and it began as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa. It became a temple after his death in 1490. The two-storey Kannon-den was started in 1482, and the sand garden's carefully formed mound is said to stand for Mount Fuji.

card.hook: Look up. There are no tangled cables across the sky here, because since 1986 the city has been taking the electric poles off Hanamikoji Street. Your photo gets clean rooflines for free.
card.stand_here: Stand on Hanamikoji Street in Gion, about 140 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. You'll look straight up the lane, with the old machiya house fronts on both sides leading you in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view down the street. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the lanterns and house fronts closer together, and save 0.5x for the tightest spots.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the rooflines level, then tap the brightest part of the street and drag the slider a touch darker so lit windows and lanterns don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, so you get the clearest view. Around dusk the lights come on and the street looks warmer, but it's usually busier.
card.selfie_here: Go to the small east-west alley near the south end of Hanamikoji. One guide calls it the most photogenic cluster of teahouses on the street, and it's nearly empty early in the morning. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the teahouses over your shoulder. For something different, Gion Tatsumi Bridge over the Shirakawa has orange planks at each end that stand out behind you, and its lanterns are lit at night.
card.ask_someone: On the quieter southern stretch toward Kennin-ji, ask someone to take your photo from the middle of the road (only when it's clear) so the whole street of old buildings fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the main street: photography is banned in the private alleys branching off Hanamikoji, with fines up to ¥10,000, so check for 'no photography' signs before entering any side lane. The houses are private too. Don't photograph, follow or ask a geiko or maiko to pose without permission. One guide says selfie sticks are banned in Gion, though that isn't officially confirmed, so keep your selfies handheld to be safe. If you stop for a photo, step aside rather than blocking the walkway.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and get one shot with the rooflines dead level and not a single cable in the sky.
card.good_to_know: Gion is Kyoto's best-known geisha district, and Hanamikoji is its best-known traditional street. It runs south from Shijō Street, where the famous Ichiriki Tei teahouse sits, down to Kennin-ji. The district is split into Gion Kobu (the larger one, which includes Hanamikoji) and the smaller Gion Higashi, which separated in 1881.

card.hook: Still water, a narrow path and trees leaning in from both sides: this is one of those spots where even a quick snap looks like you planned it. The canal does the hard work by leading the eye straight along the frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Philosopher's Path about 250 m north-west of the subject and face south-east. Stay on the path close to the water's edge, but keep clear of the walkers.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view along the canal. Switch to 0.5x when the trees arch overhead, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a stretch of blossom or the Daimonji hill.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the canal on a lower third line, so the path runs diagonally into the distance.
card.best_time: Cherry blossom season is the busiest and most colourful time. Whatever the season, going early in the day should give you a quieter path.
card.selfie_here: Find one of the small stone bridges over the canal along the middle of the path and stand on it with the stone path and trees behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and the canal reflects the flowers and trees nicely.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a public walking path beside a canal, so stay on the path and keep clear of the flow of walkers. The temples and shrines along it may have their own rules, so check the official site if you plan to visit them.
card.challenge: Wait for one lone walker to stroll into the middle distance, then snap them as your tiny scale figure.
card.good_to_know: The path began in 1890 and was extended in 1912. It runs between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji and takes about 30 minutes to walk end to end. It's named after two Kyoto University professors, Nishida Kitaro and Hajime Tanabe, who are thought to have walked it for daily exercise.

card.challenge: Shoot the lane from one end, then turn around and shoot it back. Which way wins?

card.hook: Fifteen stones, and you can never see all of them at once. That's the little joke built into Ryoan-ji's rock garden, and it's why everyone leans a bit to the left and right on the veranda.
card.stand_here: Head for the Ryoan-ji rock garden and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 35 m south-east of the numbered pin. Face north-west, toward the gravel.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole garden and the old clay wall behind it. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close shots of a stone group or the moss. Use zoom 0.5x only if you're very close, and keep the garden's edges away from the corners of the frame.
card.make_it_pop: White gravel can fool your phone, so tap the gravel, then slide the brightness down a touch until the raked lines show clearly.
card.best_time: Go when the temple opens if you can, because the veranda tends to be quieter and you can take your time. A bright overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the gravel nicely.
card.selfie_here: Our best pick is the paths around Kyoyochi Pond in the temple's outer grounds, which is a popular photo spot. It's a fallback, though: the rock garden won't be behind you there. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the pond over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the Hojo veranda while you pose there, and ask them to keep the walkway clear, then check the frame on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitor guides say flash isn't welcome here, and selfie sticks are generally not allowed at temples, so keep both in your bag. Don't stop where you block people, and keep paths and doorways clear. Check the official site for photo rules before you go.
card.challenge: Try to catch as many of the fifteen stones as you can in one shot, then count them. Can you beat the garden's little trick?
card.good_to_know: Ryoan-ji is a Zen temple in north-west Kyoto, and its dry garden is a plain rectangle of raked white gravel, about 25 metres by 10 metres, with fifteen stones in five groups. The monks rake the gravel every day, so the lines are usually crisp. Nobody is sure who made it, and the version you see today dates from a rebuild at the end of the 1700s.

card.hook: Japan's tallest wooden tower is 54.8 metres of stacked roofs, and it's too tall for your screen unless you play along. Stand upright, step back, and let it stretch.

card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the pagoda up with a vertical line, keep your phone upright, then tap the pagoda and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.

card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of Hyotan Pond with the pagoda rising behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x so the tower and its reflection both fit. In spring, the big Fuji Sakura weeping cherry near the viewing reception area puts the tree and the pagoda in one frame.

card.rules_and_safety: To-ji is a Buddhist temple and World Heritage Site, so parts may be ticketed or have set hours. Check the official site before you go. The pagoda itself is normally closed to visitors, but you can usually see inside from outside.
card.challenge: Get the whole pagoda in with a little sky above the spire and a tree or pond edge at the bottom, with no strangers in the shot. Flea market day gets bonus points.
card.good_to_know: The temple was founded in 796, soon after the capital moved to Heian-kyo. The pagoda you see now dates from 1643, when the shogun Iemitsu ordered it rebuilt, and earlier versions were destroyed several times. It became a National Treasure in 1952, and the temple is part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

card.hook: A tall, skinny pagoda looks like it's about to topple backwards the moment you tilt your phone up at it. Yasaka Pagoda is a lovely, simple vertical shape, so a steady phone gives you a shot that says 'Kyoto' at a glance.

card.hook: When fire swept through Shimo-Daigo during the Ōnin War, the five-storey pagoda was the only building left standing. It's been quietly smug about it ever since, and it makes a great photo.
card.stand_here: In Shimo-Daigo, the lower part of Daigo-ji, stand about 100 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Move a few steps either way until no passers-by block the view.

card.hook: Picture a lantern-lit alley so narrow you could nearly touch both walls, and then one block over, a wide-open river with sky above it. Pontocho gives you both, and your phone will love the contrast.

card.zoom: Start at 1x for the river and the big scene. Switch to 0.5x in the narrow alley so the lanterns and rooflines all fit, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out lanterns, signs or the riverside patios from a distance.

card.best_time: Go at dusk or early evening, when the lanterns are lit and there's still some blue left in the sky. Use night mode in the dark alley and lean against a wall or railing to keep your phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the alley mouth on the Kamo riverbank, where the lantern-lit lane meets the river, and stand one step back from the water. Use the front camera with the glowing alley behind you; Sanjo Bridge, with the river and old wooden buildings behind you, makes a nice candid backup.

card.rules_and_safety: Pontocho is very narrow, so keep any stop for photos brief and don't block the alley. Don't photograph a geiko or maiko without permission, and keep a polite distance. The restaurants, tea houses and theatre are private businesses, so check local signs.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot along the river and one close-up of lanterns and wooden fronts, then see which one your friends 'like' more.
card.good_to_know: Pontocho is a hanamachi, a traditional geisha district, and its crest is a stylised water plover, or chidori. The name is thought to come from the Portuguese word for bridge, "ponte". At the Sanjō-dōri end, the Ponto-chō Kaburenjō Theatre has hosted the annual Kamogawa Odori dance performance since the 1870s.

card.hook: Kyoto Tower has divided opinion for decades, because a smooth white spire looks pretty bold in an old capital. Lucky for you, that clash is exactly what makes the photo fun.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 100 m south of the tower, and face north. Look for a spot where the street or building edges lead your eye up towards it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, hold the phone upright and tilt up to fit the whole tower in. Keep the phone level so the tower doesn't lean. Use zoom 1x for a tighter shot of the top, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the spire and observation deck against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line one vertical line up with the spire, then put the tower slightly off-centre with a bit of street at the bottom to show how tall it is.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives you softer light and a clearer sky. If the tower is lit up after dark, try dusk with night mode on.
card.selfie_here: Head to Muromachi Koji Plaza on the west side of Kyoto Station. From the JR Central Exit, take the first escalator down and the tower is on your right. Use the front camera, then turn so the tower is over your shoulder. Karasuma Koji Plaza is another good try: from the central ticket gate, take the three far-right escalators to the top and stand on the north side. Both spots are approximate, so take a test shot and shuffle until the tower is in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The area around the tower is a city street, but the observation deck is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the spire dead straight on a grid line with a slice of street at the bottom, then take one more with you grinning in front of it.
card.good_to_know: Kyoto Tower is the tallest structure in the city, with the observation deck at 100 metres and the spire at 131 metres. It was built in 1964 on the site of the former central post office and designed to look something like a Japanese candle. Instead of an open metal lattice, it uses stacked steel rings covered in welded steel sheets.

card.hook: The red here is so loud that even a basic phone makes it look good. Add white gravel, green trees and a gate the size of a small building, and you're most of the way to a great picture.
card.stand_here: Stand about 80 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east towards the middle of Heian Shrine. Stay back far enough to fit the whole gate in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and courtyard as you see them. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you're close and want the whole gate and sky in one shot, then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof corners and painted beams.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red building, then drag the brightness slider a touch darker if the sky looks washed out, so the red stays rich and the white walls don't glare.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people, and overcast days suit that strong red. If you're there on 22 October, the Jidai Matsuri procession ends at the shrine, which adds extra colour.
card.selfie_here: Stand just inside the base of the giant vermilion torii at the entrance on Jingū-michi avenue, so the gate rises behind you and frames your head. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold it a little low so the torii and sky fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the road side of Jingū-michi avenue, south of the Grand Torii, a few steps back from the gate and facing north, while you stand in front of the gate so the whole torii fits in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is basically prohibited inside the shrine pavilions, so follow the posted signs. Drones are typically not allowed at shrines in Japan, and this is a working place of worship, so keep it respectful. The garden may be ticketed or have set opening times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch red, white and green in one frame: gate, gravel and trees. Then sneak in a second shot of one roof corner against the sky.
card.good_to_know: Heian Shrine was built for the 1895 exhibition marking 1,100 years since Kyoto (then Heian-kyō) was founded. It's a partial copy of the old Heian Palace at 5/8 of the original size, designed by Itō Chūta, and the big red gate copies the palace's Outenmon. Part of it burned down in 1976, including the main sanctuary, and it was rebuilt three years later with donations.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east towards the middle of Heian Shrine. Stay back far enough to fit the whole gate in.

card.hook: Picture a covered walkway floating in a bowl of red maples, with a crowd politely trying not to wander into your shot. That's the classic Tōfuku-ji view, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Stand on 臥雲橋 (Gaunkyo), a little north-west of the temple and about 2 minutes on foot from it, so the temple lies to the south-east of you. Face back up the Sengyokukan ravine and you'll see the covered Tsutenkyo walkway framed by the maples.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to take in the whole ravine with the walkway in the middle. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the walkway and its trees. Use 0.5x only if the bridge is packed and you want a wider scene.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest leaves, then slide the brightness down a touch so the reds stay rich instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the light is soft and the crowds are thinner. Mid-November to early December is the peak autumn season and the busiest time.
card.selfie_here: Take it right on Gaunkyo Bridge, which is free to cross and sits before the ticket gate. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn so Tsutenkyo and the maple valley are behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Gaunkyo Bridge facing up toward Tsutenkyo, so you and the whole bridge with the maple ravine fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are banned, so hold your phone in your hand. In the autumn special viewing, photography on the bridges may be restricted and you may be asked to refrain, so check the official site and follow the staff. Don't lean over the edge, and keep to your lane.
card.challenge: Line the walkway up with a gridline so it sits level, then get one shot with no stranger's elbow in it. Good luck.
card.good_to_know: Tōfuku-ji was founded in 1236 by the imperial chancellor Kujō Michiie and is one of Kyoto's five great Zen temples, the Kyoto Gozan. Its main gate is the oldest sanmon in Japan and a National Treasure. Today the complex has 24 sub-temples.

card.hook: Higashi Hongan-ji has one real problem: the main hall is so big you'll spend your first minute just backing up. Locals call the temple Ohigashisan, 'Honorable Mr. East', which sounds like a friendly neighbour with a very large roof.
card.stand_here: Stand about 120 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west towards the Goei-dō. Step back until the whole roofline fits on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full width of the Goei-dō with a bit of sky, then try 1x for a calmer, more balanced view of the front. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) picks out roof ends, carved timber and lanterns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roof ridge up with a horizontal line so the giant hall doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the dark timber and fewer people in the courtyard. Midday makes harsh shadows under the deep roofs, so skip it if you can.
card.selfie_here: Head to the cherry tree at the entrance of Mieido Hall, inside the temple grounds. A Trip.com guide names it as the most iconic photo spot here, with the hall as your backdrop. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the hall over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On Karasuma-dori heading north, ask a passer-by to stand back on the street with the Goeidomon Gate straight ahead of them, while you pose with the gate behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the halls, including the Goei-dō, because they're active places of worship. Elsewhere, follow any signs, and keep your voice and phone low during services.
card.challenge: Get the roof ridge perfectly level on a gridline, with one tiny person in the courtyard to show just how huge the hall is.
card.good_to_know: The Goei-dō is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world: 76 metres long, 58 metres wide and 38 metres high. The hall you see today dates from 1895, after a long run of fires. The temple itself was founded in 1602 by the shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 120 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west towards the Goei-dō. Step back until the whole roofline fits on your screen.

card.hook: Water, trees and old-style rooftops all squeezed into one frame: Shinsen-en is a gift if all you've got is a phone. You get layers and reflections without fiddling with anything.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big view of the garden. Tap 0.5x if the space is tight and you can't step back, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for lanterns, leaves and reflections.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then drag it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the water keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer. Midday sun can make harsh patches under the trees.
